title: Why Sensible People Follow the Crowd, and Why Crowds Can Turn on a Dime
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: A Theory of Fads, Fashion, Custom, and Cultural Change as Informational Cascades
source.authors: Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer, and Ivo Welch

intro.summary: The core paper (Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch, 1992) asks why people so often end up doing the same thing, and why that shared behaviour can collapse suddenly. Its model has people decide one after another. Each has a private, imperfect clue and can see only what earlier people did. The authors show that after only a couple of matching choices, it becomes rational to copy the crowd and ignore your own clue. From then on, the crowd's choices carry no new information, so these 'cascades' are often wrong and are easily broken by a little public news. A later physics paper (Hisakado and Mori) extends the idea to voters who copy a few others in a network. It finds that once copiers pass a critical share, the crowd can lock onto either the right or the wrong answer, and that network hubs barely move that tipping point. The main limits: the core results are mathematical models with illustrative examples rather than tests, the authors themselves call some predictions unrealistic, and the network results rest on approximations and finite simulations. Good follow-up topics are lab tests that try to separate cascades from simple herding, fads that arise when the true value can change, 'fashion leaders' with better information, and cascades on small-world networks.
background: A private signal is a clue only you see, such as a taste test, a hunch or a review you read, and it is right more often than wrong but not always.
Updating on evidence (Bayes' rule) means each new clue shifts how likely you think something is, and independent clues add up.
Copying others can be a sensible way to learn, because their choices may reflect clues you do not have.
The core paper is a mathematical model; the stories it cites (hybrid corn, tonsillectomy, sage grouse) are illustrations, not proof.
intro.aha: A crowd of millions in a cascade may rest on just two people's clues, so it is wrong surprisingly often, and one small piece of public news, weaker than a single person's clue, can overturn it.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Whole groups often converge on one behaviour: a restaurant, a medical procedure, a political mood. Older theories explained this with punishment for being different, benefits from matching others, or a simple liking for fitting in. Those forces make conformity sturdier the longer it lasts. But real fashions and fads often flip suddenly. The authors wanted one explanation for both the sameness and the sudden flips.
primer.quote: None of these theories explains why mass behavior is often fragile in the sense that small shocks can frequently lead to large shifts in behavior.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They built a simple model. People line up and each decides to adopt or reject something, such as a new seed or a treatment. Each person has a private clue that points the right way more often than not. Each person sees what everyone before them chose, but not their clues. Everyone reasons sensibly from what they can see. Then the authors worked out what the line of choices looks like.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: Very quickly, often by the third person, the evidence from earlier choices outweighs any single private clue. From then on everyone copies, whatever their own clue says. This is an informational cascade. Because copiers ignore their clues, their choices add nothing new. The whole crowd may rest on two or three early clues, so it can easily be wrong. A lab version with urns and coloured balls, run by Anderson and Holt, found cascades in most rounds.
primer.quote: The experimenters observed that an information cascade was observed in 41 of 56 such runs.

primer.heading: Why crowds are fragile
primer.body: Since a cascade holds only a little real information, a little new public information can break it, even after millions have joined. This explains why fads appear and vanish. It also suggests why it can be worth publishing even modest evidence against a popular practice. One caution: the authors note that real life mixes cascades with peer pressure, payoffs from matching and the wish to fit in.
primer.quote: Intuitively, cascades aggregate the information of only a few early individuals' actions.
primer.quote_where: Section III.A.2, The Depth of a Cascade

primer.heading: Crowds and networks
primer.body: A later physics paper by Hisakado and Mori mixes 'independents', who follow their own clue, with 'herders', who copy the majority of a few earlier voters picked through a network. Once herders pass a critical share, the vote can settle on either the right or the wrong answer. Networks with big hubs change how fast the vote settles but not that tipping point. These results come from approximations and computer simulations, not from real voting data.
primer.quote: In our model the network does not affect the critical point at which an information cascade transition occurs.

concepts.title: Clues add up: how evidence shifts your belief
concepts.idea: With equally reliable yes/no clues, your belief that something is good depends only on how many more 'good' clues than 'bad' clues you have, and on how reliable each clue is.

predict.question: Maya's clues are each right 80% of the time. She has two good clues and no bad ones. Then she gets one more good clue and one more bad clue. What happens to her chance that the thing is good?
options: It stays exactly where it was
It goes up: she now has three good clues
It goes down: the bad clue is the newest news
It drops to 50%: mixed evidence means no idea
why: Right. The new good clue and the new bad clue cancel, so her lead is still two, and with the same reliability her belief is unchanged.
Counting only the good clues is tempting, but the new bad clue cancels the new good one. Only the lead counts, and it is still two.
Recent news can feel weightier, but in this model order does not matter. Each clue counts the same, and the pair cancels.
Her evidence is mixed overall, but she still has two more good clues than bad ones. Belief returns to 50% only when the lead is zero.

terms.means: The rule of probability for updating a belief when new evidence arrives
Your belief after weighing the clues, written as a chance
How often a single clue points the right way. 50% means the clue is useless.

model.title: How likely is it good, given the clues you hold?
model.note: Teaching model: one person starts at 50–50 and gets yes/no clues. Each clue is right with the same chance, and clues are independent of one another once the truth is fixed. The person combines them by the laws of probability, as in the binary-clue case of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992) with a 50–50 starting belief. Clue counts and settings are illustrative, not data from the paper.

controls.label: How often a clue is right

steps.say: Two bars: how likely something is good, and how likely it is bad. With no clues at all, it's a coin toss, 50–50.
This slider hands you good clues, hints that it's good. One clue tips the bars.
This one hands you bad clues, hints the other way.
This slider sets how often a single clue is right. Trust your clues more, and one clue moves you further.
This box counts good clues minus bad ones. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: Play with the clue counts and their reliability. See how many different clue piles you can find that land on the same belief.

goals.text: Hold at least four clues, each better than a coin toss, and still be exactly 50–50.
hints: What happens to your belief when a good clue meets a bad clue?
Each bad clue cancels exactly one good clue. Watch the lead box.
Give both clue sliders the same count, high enough that together they make at least four.

goals.text: With at least five bad clues on the table, push the chance it's good above 90%.
hints: Five bad clues pull hard. What could outweigh them?
Only the lead and the reliability matter. You need several more good clues than bad ones, or clues you can trust more.
At the starting reliability, grow the lead one good clue at a time and watch where the good bar passes 90%.

feedback.correct: Yes. A good clue and a bad clue of equal reliability cancel exactly, so Maya's lead stays at two and her belief does not move.
feedback.incorrect: It is natural to weigh the newest clue more, or to count only good clues. In this model each clue shifts the odds by the same factor, up for good and down for bad, so one of each leaves the lead and the belief unchanged.

steps.say: One good clue, and each clue is right 70% of the time. Your belief jumps from 50% to 70%. Updating a belief from evidence like this follows Bayes' rule, and the result is your posterior.
A second good clue pushes the posterior higher, to about 84%.
Now add one bad clue. You're back at 70%, exactly where one good clue left you.
Three good and two bad: still 70%. Each matching pair cancels. Only the lead of one is left.
Even them up at three and three: 50%. Six clues, and you know no more than with none.
The second ingredient is signal accuracy, how often a clue is right. With a lead of two but clues right only 55% of the time, you're barely past 60%.
Keep the same lead of two, but make the clues right 90% of the time. Now you're near 99%.
Pile on clues: eight good, six bad. The lead is still two, and the belief is the same 99%. The size of the pile doesn't count. Only the lead and the accuracy do.

understand.explanation: Each good clue multiplies the odds that the thing is good by the same factor, and each bad clue divides them by that same factor. So a good clue and a bad clue cancel exactly. Your belief depends only on the lead (good minus bad) and on how reliable each clue is. Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992) build their cascade model on this arithmetic: a person holding one good and one bad clue is exactly 50–50. The Wikipedia summary writes out the same Bayes' rule calculation for any number of clues. All of this holds only under the model's assumptions: equally reliable clues, clues independent of one another given the truth, and a person who reasons perfectly. Real people often update less neatly.
understand.quote: If the first individual adopted, the second individual adopts if his signal is also H. However, if his signal is L, the second individual computes the expected value of adoption (given one H and one L signal) to be 1/2.

connect.caption: This is the Bayes' rule formula from the Wikipedia summary, with the starting belief set to 50–50 so it cancels out. Wikipedia's q is the slider 'How often a clue is right' (the 1992 paper calls it p). a counts good clues and b counts bad clues. The result is the 'Chance it's good' bar. Divide top and bottom by the matching pairs and only a − b, the lead, is left.

concepts.recap: Matching good and bad clues cancel: your belief rests only on the lead and on how trustworthy each clue is.

concepts.title: Two matching choices outweigh your own clue
concepts.idea: When you can see only earlier actions, you infer their clues from those actions, and once adopters lead rejecters by two, your single clue can no longer change your choice, so you copy.

predict.question: Suppose every clue is much sharper, right 95% of the time instead of 70%. Everyone else is the same. How big a lead of earlier adopters over rejecters do you now need before you would ignore your own bad clue and adopt anyway?
options: A lead of one is enough
A bigger lead, because a 95%-right clue is hard to override
No lead is ever enough: with clues that good you always trust your own
why: Tempting, because sharper clues make each earlier choice look more convincing. But a lead of one only cancels your one bad clue and leaves you at 50–50, so you toss a coin. You don't copy for sure.
Right. Each earlier choice is read as a clue exactly as sharp as yours, so sharper clues strengthen both sides equally. Only the count matters, and two beats one at any accuracy above 50%.
This feels natural, since a reliable clue deserves respect. But the earlier people's clues are just as reliable, so two of them still outweigh your sharper one.
This would hold only if your clue were better than everyone else's. In this model all clues are equally good, so two earlier ones still outvote yours.

terms.means: The point where what earlier people did outweighs your own clue, so your choice no longer depends on that clue
A cascade in which everyone from then on adopts
A cascade in which everyone from then on rejects

model.title: Earlier choices plus your own clue: what do you do?
model.note: Teaching model: the binary-clue case of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992). Everyone starts at 50–50, and every clue is right with the same chance. You adopt if 'good' is more likely than 'bad', reject if less likely, and toss a coin on a tie. 'Good clues' and 'Bad clues' now count earlier people who adopted or rejected while still following their own clue; each such choice is read as one clue. In the paper, a choice made on a coin-flip tie reveals a little less than a full clue, but this does not change where copying starts. Choices made by people who were already copying reveal nothing, so in a real queue the lead you can read from choices stops at two. Settings are illustrative, not data from the paper.

controls.label: How often a clue is right

outputs.label: Chance I'd adopt with the opposite clue
How much my clue swings my choice

bars.label: Chance I'd adopt with the opposite clue

steps.say: Same belief bars as before, with one twist: you can't see other people's clues, only what they did. 'Good clues' now counts earlier people who adopted. 'Bad clues' counts those who rejected.
New switch: your own private clue, good or bad. The good and bad bars now include it on top of the earlier choices.
Two new bars show what you'd do: once with your clue as set, once with the opposite clue. If they differ, your clue matters.

explore.prompt: You're somewhere in a queue, watching earlier choices. Arrange the queue so your own clue gets overruled.

goals.text: Find a queue where you would adopt for sure, even though your own clue says bad.
hints: Your bad clue counts as one clue against adopting. What would the earlier choices need to show to beat it outright?
If the earlier adopters only cancel your bad clue, you land on 50–50 and toss a coin. Watch the 'Chance I adopt' bar.
Switch your clue to bad, keep the rejecters at zero, and add adopters one at a time until the adopt bar reaches 100%.

goals.text: Now the other direction. With earlier people rejecting, make your own clue make no difference at all, using as few earlier choices as possible.
hints: This time the earlier people should mostly reject, and your switch should not change what you do.
Watch 'How much my clue swings my choice'. You want it at 0%. Flip your switch both ways to check.
Use only rejecters, add them one at a time, and stop at the first count where the swing drops to 0%.

feedback.correct: Yes. Sharper clues make both sides sharper together, because each earlier choice is read as a clue as good as yours. The decision depends only on the count, so a lead of two overrules your one clue at any accuracy.
feedback.incorrect: It's easy to think a very reliable clue should be harder to override. But here the earlier people's clues are exactly as reliable as yours, so accuracy cancels out. Two clues read from earlier choices beat your one clue whatever the accuracy.

steps.say: Start at the front of the queue. Nobody has chosen yet, so the lead is zero. Your good clue says adopt, and you adopt.
Flip your clue to bad and you reject. When you go first, your clue decides everything: the swing is 100%.
Now one person adopted before you. They were following their own clue, so their adopting tells you their clue was good. Read their action as one good clue.
Flip your clue to bad. Their good clue and your bad one cancel to 50–50, so you toss a coin. Your clue still matters, but only halfway.
Two people adopted ahead of you. With a good clue you adopt, of course.
Now flip your clue to bad. Two good minus one bad still leaves good ahead, so you adopt anyway. Both decision bars sit at 100%, and your clue's swing is 0%.

This is an informational cascade: your choice no longer depends on your own clue. Since you adopt either way, anyone watching learns nothing about your clue. Everyone adopts here, so this is an up cascade.
It works in reverse too. After two rejections, even a good clue leads you to reject. That's a down cascade.

understand.explanation: In the paper's simple model, you see only what earlier people did, never their clues. While those people were following their own clues, each choice reveals a clue, so choices add up just like the clues in the last concept. Your private clue counts as exactly one clue of the same strength. So once adopters lead rejecters by two, your bad clue can only cut the lead to one, and you adopt either way. That is an up cascade; two more rejections than adoptions starts a down cascade in the same way. The authors stress that this copying is a rational use of the evidence you can see, not peer pressure or a taste for fitting in. They showed it by working through the choices person by person in a mathematical model. It is a theory result, not an experiment, and it assumes all clues are equally reliable.
understand.quote: The third individual is faced with one of three situations: (1) both predecessors have adopted (in which case even an L signal induces him to adopt and thus creates an up cascade)

connect.caption: This is the model's rule. It matches the paper's Bayes calculation for its binary-clue case, with a 50–50 start and a cost of ½. p is how often a clue is right. The lead is earlier adopters minus rejecters, each read as one clue. ± 1 is your own clue: +1 if good, −1 if bad. Once the lead is two or more, ± 1 can't push the result across ½, so your clue stops mattering.

concepts.recap: Once earlier choices lead by two, your one clue can't tip the balance, so you copy and a cascade begins.

concepts.title: Cascades stop learning, so they are often wrong
concepts.idea: Once a cascade starts, later choices carry no information, so the crowd's final answer rests on a few early clues and ends up wrong surprisingly often, even when clues are fairly accurate.

predict.question: A town of 10,000 people try a new restaurant one at a time. Each sees only who went in, and each has a private clue that is right 80% of the time. Compare it with a village of 100 doing the same. What is the town's chance of locking onto the wrong answer?
options: Much lower: 10,000 clues should outvote a few bad early ones
About the same as the village, roughly 1 in 7
Higher: a longer line gives more chances to go wrong
why: This is tempting because 10,000 clues really do exist. But once the line locks in, everyone copies, and copies reveal nothing. The extra clues are never pooled, so the answer still rests on the first few.

Right. In both places the line almost surely locks in within the first handful of people. What happens after that adds no evidence. With 80% clues, the paper's formula gives about a 14% chance of a wrong lock-in, whether 100 or 10,000 people follow.

This is tempting because more people means more decisions. But after the lock-in, every later person copies whatever came first, so a longer line cannot drift into a new mistake. It only repeats the old one.

terms.means: Pooling many people's private clues so the group knows more than any one person
A cascade in which everyone copies the wrong choice

model.title: Where does a line of choosers end up?
model.note: Teaching model: these curves are the paper's exact formulas (its equation 3) for its simplest case. The choice is yes/no, and 'good' and 'bad' start equally likely. Everyone's clue is equally accurate, everyone sees all earlier choices, ties are broken by a coin flip, and the true answer is 'good'. As in the paper's formula, crowd size moves in even numbers. The percentages are calculated from that formula. They are not measurements of real crowds.

controls.label: How often each private clue is right
People who have chosen so far

x.label: How often each private clue is right

steps.say: Picture a line of people choosing yes or no. Each sees only the earlier choices. This upper curve is the chance the line locks onto the right answer.
This lower curve is the chance it locks onto the wrong answer.
Going left to right, private clues get more reliable: from a coin toss up to always right. This slider picks one accuracy, and the vertical line marks it.
This slider sets how many people have chosen so far. The dashed curve is the chance the line hasn't locked in yet.
These boxes read off all three chances at your setting.

explore.prompt: You've seen that a locked-in line stops learning. Now find where the risk of a wrong answer really sits: in the clues, or in the size of the crowd?

goals.text: Find the least accurate clues at which a fully settled line locks onto the wrong answer less than 1 time in 10.
hints: Once the line has settled, crowd size barely moves the wrong-answer chance. Which slider does?
Raise clue accuracy a step at a time from 70% and watch the wrong-answer box.
It drops under 1 in 10 somewhere in the mid-80s. Stop at the first step that gets there.

goals.text: Find a setting where the line has almost surely locked in, yet it lands on the wrong answer more than 1 time in 3.
hints: Wrong lock-ins get more likely as clues get worse.
Lower clue accuracy, but keep enough people in line that the dashed 'not locked in yet' chance stays under 1%.
Clues only a little better than a coin toss will do it. Check the dashed box stays tiny.

feedback.correct: Yes. After the first few choices the line locks in, and every later choice is a copy that reveals nothing. A town and a village end up resting on the same handful of early clues, so the wrong-answer risk is about the same.
feedback.incorrect: You probably pictured each person adding their clue to a growing pile. When only choices can be seen, that pile stops growing as soon as the line locks in. More people just means more copies, not more evidence.

steps.say: Start with useless clues, right only half the time. Ten people in, the line has almost surely locked in, but it's a coin flip: about 50% right, 50% wrong.
Rewind to just two people. Even here, three times in four the line has already locked in. Lock-ins happen fast.
Now give everyone clues that are right 70% of the time. Ten people in, the line is almost surely locked in. Yet about one time in four it has locked onto the wrong answer.
Double the line to twenty people. The wrong-answer chance doesn't budge. Once the line locks in, each new choice is a copy, and a copy tells later people nothing about the copier's own clue.
So twenty private clues exist, but only the first few ever count. Pooling everyone's clues is called information aggregation. Here it simply stops at the moment of lock-in.
Sharpen the clues to 90% right. The wrong chance falls, but it is still about 6%. A whole crowd of good judges can still march off together in the wrong direction.
A line locked onto the wrong answer is called a reverse cascade. At 75%-accurate clues the formula gives about 81% right and 19% wrong. Notice how slowly the lower curve sinks as clues improve.

understand.explanation: When people can see only earlier choices, the first two or three choices decide where the line locks in. After that, everyone copies, so each new choice reveals nothing about that person's own clue, and learning stops. The crowd's answer therefore rests on a handful of early clues, and a handful of clues is often misleading. With 70%-accurate clues, the paper's formula gives roughly a 1-in-4 chance of locking onto the wrong answer, no matter how many people follow. The paper derives exact chances of right and wrong lock-ins for this yes/no model and shows the right-answer chance rises only gradually with clue accuracy. Its later table puts it at about 0.81 for 75%-accurate clues after 1,000 people. These are results of a stylised model with identical people and equally accurate clues, not measurements of real crowds.
understand.quote: The first expression is the probability of the correct cascade. It can be shown that this probability is increasing in p (see fig. 1) and n. Even for very informative signals (where p is far from 1/2), the probability of the wrong cascade is remarkably high.
understand.quote_where: Section II.A (A Specific Model), after equation (3)

check.task: Put the model in a state where the line has almost surely locked in (under 1% not locked in yet) and a wrong lock-in is less likely than 1 in 20.
check.hint: Adding people only shrinks the dashed curve. Which slider actually lowers the solid wrong-answer curve, and how far must it go?
check.misconception: A bigger crowd washes out early mistakes, so with enough people a wrong lock-in becomes rare. In fact, once the line has settled, only sharper private clues lower the risk.

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation (3) for the case where the true answer is 'good'. p is how often a private clue is right (the paper's p), and n is how many people have chosen. The term (p − p²)^{n/2} is the chance the line hasn't locked in yet, which shrinks fast as n grows. That is why n barely matters once the line has settled. The wrong-lock-in chance has the same form with (2 − p)(1 − p) in place of p(p + 1).

concepts.recap: When only choices can be seen, a crowd's answer rests on its first few clues, so it can lock onto the wrong answer even with good clues and huge numbers.

activities.prompt: Same people, same private clues. The only difference is what later people can see. The paper notes the two worlds behave identically right up until a cascade begins.

cases.label: Everyone's clues are visible
cases.text: Each person's clue joins a shared pool, even if they don't act on it. A long enough run of opposing clues eventually flips behaviour, so as the line grows, the crowd heads toward the right answer.

cases.label: Only choices are visible
cases.text: Once two more people have chosen one way than the other, everyone copies. Copies reveal nothing, so the pool stops at a few clues. In this basic model a lock-in, right or wrong, is never undone.

activities.takeaway: Seeing only actions makes the crowd more uniform, but it freezes the evidence early. That frozen early evidence is what makes wrong lock-ins common.

concepts.title: Too many copiers: when a crowd can lock onto the wrong answer
concepts.idea: With copiers who follow the majority of three earlier voters, raising their share past a critical point (2/3 in the simplest case) creates two stable outcomes: one mostly right, one mostly wrong.

predict.question: In this lesson each copier looked at three earlier votes picked at random. Now suppose copiers mostly look at a few popular 'hub' voters that many others also watch, like influencers on a social network. What happens to the copier share at which the mostly-wrong outcome first appears?
options: It stays the same. Hubs change how fast the vote settles, not where the split happens
It drops. A few hubs let the crowd lock onto the wrong answer with fewer copiers
It rises. Hubs spread more information, so more copiers are needed
It disappears. With hubs there is only ever one resting place
why: This matches the paper. For hub-heavy networks (the Barabási–Albert and fitness models), the long-run balance equation came out identical to the random case, so the tipping point is the same. Hubs only made the vote settle more slowly.

Influencers seem powerful, so this is a natural guess. But in the paper, the votes a hub's followers see end up, over time, split the same way as the whole crowd. The same balance equation appears, and so does the same tipping point.
Hubs add no new independent information here: they are just voters whom others happen to watch. The paper found no shift in the tipping point in either direction.
The two-outcome split survived on hub networks, both in the math and in the simulations. The case with no split is different: copiers who look only at the most recent voters, in a chain.

terms.means: The paper's name for a copier: a voter who follows the majority of the earlier votes they look at
A resting place the vote drifts back to after a small nudge. The paper calls the two of them good and bad equilibria
The copier share at which one resting place splits into three (written p_c)
The paper's name for that split, from one likely outcome to two coexisting ones

model.title: Where the next vote's chance meets the vote so far
model.note: Teaching model: this plots the paper's long-run balance equation for copiers who check three earlier votes picked at random (the random-graph case, r = 3). As in the paper, those three votes are treated as drawn with replacement, an averaged (mean-field) approximation. It shows where the vote can come to rest. It does not show how fast the vote gets there, or which resting place a particular crowd reaches. The curve follows the paper's equation; the slider settings are illustrative, not reported data.

controls.label: How often an independent voter is right

outputs.label: Places the vote can come to rest

x.label: Share picking the right answer so far

y.label: Next voter's chance of picking right

series.label: Next voter's chance of picking right
No change: chance equals share so far

steps.say: The S-shaped curve gives the chance that the next voter picks the right answer. It depends on how the vote stands so far, read from left to right.
The dashed line means 'no change'. Where the curve crosses it, the vote keeps its current share. That crossing is a place the vote can come to rest.
This slider sets the share of copiers, who look at three earlier votes and follow the majority. Watch the curve bend.
This one sets how often everyone else, who decides alone, picks the right answer.
These boxes count the resting places and show where the highest and lowest ones sit.

explore.prompt: Hunt down the tipping point, then see how it moves when the independent voters know more.

goals.text: Keep the independents as coin flips, and find the fewest copiers that still give the vote two places to rest.
hints: The split happens when the middle of the S becomes steeper than the dashed line.
Start with plenty of copiers, where you can see two outer dots. Then lower the copier share one step at a time until they merge back into one.
Stop one step above where the outer dots merge. It lies between the two copier shares the walkthrough used with coin-flip independents.

goals.text: Make the independents right at least three times in four, yet still leave room for a mostly-wrong outcome.
hints: Better-informed independents lift the low end of the curve, which makes a low crossing harder to create.
Set the independents first. Then raise the copier share until a dot appears below the halfway mark.
Expect the tipping point to sit higher than it did with independents who were right 60% of the time.

feedback.correct: Right. The paper re-derived the balance for copiers who watch popular voters (the Barabási–Albert and fitness models, which have strong hubs). The equation came out identical to the random case, and the simulations put the critical point in the same place. Hubs changed only how quickly the vote settled, which was always slower, so the authors conclude that hubs have limited influence.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think influencers swing the crowd. But in this model a copier's three votes, hub or not, end up split roughly the same way as the whole crowd. So the same balance equation and the same tipping point appear. The paper found that hubs affected only the speed of settling, and its simulations had to contend with large finite-size effects.

steps.say: Start with no copiers and independents who are pure coin flips. The curve is flat at 50%: whatever the count so far, the next voter is 50/50. It meets the dashed line once, at 50%.
Now add copiers, which the paper calls herders. The flat line bends into an S. When one answer leads, a herder usually sees a majority for it among the three votes they check, and adds one more.
There is still one crossing. In the middle, the S is flatter than the dashed line. So if the vote drifts above 50%, the next voter's chance falls below the current share, and the vote slides back.
Past two-thirds copiers, the middle of the S becomes steeper than the dashed line. The single crossing splits into three.
Each outer crossing is a stable outcome: nudge the vote and it drifts back. The middle one is a knife edge, and the vote rolls off it to one side or the other.
The copier share where the split first happens is the critical point. The paper calls the split the information cascade transition. Early luck now decides which side a crowd lands on.
Now let independents be right 60% of the time, with moderate copying. There is one resting place, near three-quarters right: the copiers amplify the truth.

Push the copiers to 85%. A mostly-wrong resting place appears, where only about one voter in eight is right. It sits beside one where over nine in ten are right, even though every independent leans toward the truth.

understand.explanation: In Hisakado and Mori's voting model, independent voters pick the right answer with a fixed chance, while herders look at three earlier votes and follow their majority. Over a long run, the share voting right must reproduce itself, which happens where the S-curve meets the dashed line. With few herders there is one such place. Past a critical point (2/3 when independents are coin flips, and higher when they lean right), there are two, each a stable outcome: one mostly right and one mostly wrong, with a knife edge between them. As with the cascades you saw earlier, chance in the early votes decides which one a crowd reaches. The paper derives this from an averaged (mean-field) equation that treats the three votes as drawn with replacement. Its simulations locate the same tipping point, though finite-size effects near it are large, and copiers who look at only one or two votes produce no split at all.
understand.quote: If the voter obtains information from three of the above voters, as the number of herders increases, the model features a phase transition beyond which the state in which most voters make the correct choice coexists with one in which most of them are wrong.

connect.caption: The paper's long-run balance (eq. 59) for r = 3. Z is the share picking right. The left side is the dashed line; the right side is the S-curve. Independents add q(1 − p), where q is the independents' accuracy and p is the copier share. Copiers add p·π(Z), where π(Z) is the chance that a random three-vote sample favours the right answer (eq. 3). Each crossing of the two sides is a solution.

concepts.recap: Past a critical share of copiers (2/3 with coin-flip independents and three-vote checks), a second, mostly-wrong resting place appears, and early luck picks which one the crowd reaches.

concepts.title: A whisper can topple millions
concepts.idea: Because a cascade holds only about two people's worth of evidence however many follow it, one public clue weaker than a single private clue is enough to make the next person use their own clue again and possibly reverse the crowd.

predict.question: Two towns each have an up cascade. In town A, 10 people have followed it. In town B, two million have. The same faint public news against adopting, weaker than one private clue, reaches the next person in each town. Where is that person more likely to start using their own clue again?
options: Town A: a small cascade is easier to shake
Town B: a huge cascade looks suspicious
Neither: faint news can never break a cascade
why: It feels natural that more people means more evidence. But everyone after the first two choices was copying, so both cascades rest on the same thin evidence.
Size doesn't make a cascade look suspicious in this model. The two million extra choices carry no information either way, so they can't raise doubt or settle it.
Right. The followers revealed nothing, so each town's cascade holds the same less-than-two clues from its first two choices. The same news tips both by exactly the same amount.
This would be true if the news had to outweigh the whole crowd. It only has to outweigh the thin evidence of the first two choices, and a clue weaker than one private clue can do that.

terms.means: A clue that everyone sees at once, such as a published study, as opposed to a private clue only one person has

model.title: Earlier choices plus your own clue: what changes after one piece of news?
model.note: Teaching model: the binary-clue case of Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1992), as on the last screen. Everyone starts at 50–50, every private clue is right with the same chance, and ties are settled by a coin toss. 'Good clues' and 'Bad clues' count earlier adoptions and rejections, read the way the paper reads them. While the lead is one or less, each choice counts as a full clue. Once one side leads by two, the choice that made it two may have come from a coin toss, so it counts for less than a full clue. Every choice after that is a copy that reveals nothing, so a lead past two changes nothing. The news is fixed: it always points against the crowd's lead (there is none with no lead) and is worth half a private clue. For every clue accuracy on the slider, that is weaker than one private clue but stronger than the coin-toss choice, the window the paper's Result 3 describes. Settings are illustrative, not data from the paper.

goals.text: Build an up cascade where, without news, the next person copies whatever their clue says, but after the news their own clue decides.
hints: Copying starts at a certain lead of adopters over rejecters. What was it?
Without news, the first two bars should match. After the news, the two choice bars should split apart.
Raise the adopters one at a time from where they start, watching the opposite-clue bar with no news reach 100%.

goals.text: Now build a long down cascade, with rejecters at least six ahead, where the news against the crowd still hands the choice back to the next person's own clue.
hints: Which slider builds a crowd that rejects?
Without news, both no-news bars should sit at 0%. After the news, which here says 'good', your clue should matter again.
Make sure adopters don't eat into the rejecters' lead: the lead is what counts, not the totals.

feedback.correct: Yes. Everyone after the first two choices copied, so their choices revealed nothing. A cascade of two million holds exactly the same evidence as one of ten, and the same faint news tips both.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to treat a bigger crowd as more evidence, but in a cascade the followers ignore their own clues. Their choices add nothing, so the cascade's evidence stays at the first two choices however long it runs. The news has the same effect in both towns.

steps.say: Two adopters, no rejecters. Without news this is an up cascade: even with a bad clue you'd adopt. See the second bar at 100%.
How much do those two choices really reveal? About 1.32 clues, not 2. The second adopter might have had a bad clue and tossed a coin, so that choice counts for less.
Now let six more people adopt. They were copying, so their choices reveal nothing. The box stays at 1.32.

Look right. After news worth just half a private clue, the opposite-clue bar drops to 0%: a bad clue would now make you reject. Your own clue decides again. News that everyone sees, like this, is what the paper calls public information.
Flip your own clue to bad. Without news you'd still adopt, but after the news you reject. Your choice now tells later people something, so the crowd can start to turn.
It works the other way too. Eight rejecters, and now the news says 'good'. Once again, half a clue gives your own clue back its say.

Here is the punchline. Eight followers, or eight million, rest on about 1.3 clues. That's why such crowds are wrong surprisingly often, and why news weaker than one person's clue can tip them. The paper calls this fragility.

understand.explanation: Once one choice leads by two, everyone after copies. Their choices add nothing, so the whole crowd rests on its first two choices, and because the second may have come from a coin toss, those two together are worth less than two clues. Public news only has to outweigh that thin layer of evidence, not the crowd. In their binary-clue model, the authors show that one public clue slightly less informative than a single private clue makes the next person go back to their own clue. Their choice then reveals that clue to later people, so the cascade may reverse. This holds however many have followed: the authors write 'even if millions subsequently imitated'. It is a theoretical result from a stylised model, and the paper offers cases such as the oat bran fad and hybrid corn adoption as possible illustrations, not as tests.
understand.quote: The release of a small amount of public information can shatter a long-lasting cascade, where a "small amount" refers to a signal less informative than the private signal of a single individual.

check.task: Build an up cascade at least seven adopters long in which, after the news, the next person rejects.
check.hint: The news alone doesn't decide; it hands the choice back to the person's own clue. What must that clue say for them to reject?
check.misconception: That a long cascade needs evidence as big as the crowd to shake it. Half a clue of news hands the choice back to the person's own clue, however many copied, and a bad clue then means rejecting.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, built from the paper's binary-clue case; the paper argues Result 3 in words. R (teal) is what earlier choices reveal, capped at 1 + ln((1+p)/(2−p)) / ln(p/(1−p)) clues however long the queue. ±1 is your own clue, and ∓½ is the news, half a clue against the crowd's lead. p is clue accuracy, as in the paper. You adopt when the log-odds are above zero and toss a coin at zero.

concepts.recap: A cascade of millions may rest on the first two choices, so it is often wrong, and news weaker than one person's clue can hand the choice back to private clues and overturn it.
